title: China's MIIT sets 9,800-exaflop 2030 compute target, ¥3.8T infrastructure budget
subtitle: Beijing laid out an explicit five-year AI-compute quadrupling plan, tying it to a ¥3.8 trillion IT infrastructure commitment and framing domestic tooling as the primary constraint.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology published the 15th Five-Year Plan for information and communications on September 7, 2026, with detailed reporting landing over the following 48 hours. The plan targets 9,800 exaflops of intelligent compute by 2030, against 2,185 exaflops recorded at the end of June 2026 and 1,590 exaflops at end-2025. It commits ¥3.8 trillion (approximately US$532 billion) in cumulative IT infrastructure spending across 2026–2030, paired with an advanced-storage target of 1,700 exabytes by 2030. The plan calls for the 'orderly deployment' of 10,000-card and 100,000-card GPU clusters and names domestic-accelerator adaptation — Huawei Ascend, Cambricon, and newer entrants — as the primary substitution path against continuing US export controls.

The number that matters is the ratio. 9,800 exaflops in 2030 is roughly 4.5x the current base and lands in the same order of magnitude as US public estimates of domestic AI compute for the same year, which vary depending on whether Nvidia's committed but not-yet-installed capacity is counted. If Beijing hits the target, the US–China compute gap that has been the operative assumption in Washington policy since the 2022 export controls closes to something closer to parity — with the gap sitting inside chip generation, not chip count.

Broader context: the announcement follows DeepSeek's September 7 disclosure of a 160,000-unit Huawei Ascend 950DT deployment in Inner Mongolia and MoE inference-chip pivots at Alibaba and Meituan-owned Longcat. Read together with the parallel-purchase policy Beijing has enforced through 2026 — every imported Western accelerator paired with a domestic equivalent — the MIIT plan reads as the demand-side counterpart to a supply-side buildout that is already three quarters underway. The AI Basic Act in South Korea, the EU's AI Gigafactory tenders, and the Trump administration's Frontier AI Framework EO now all have Chinese-side counterparts.

Takeaway for learners: 'compute' is the unit that AI industrial policy actually trades in, and reading these plans is a much better guide to what shapes the market than following model-release headlines. If you are studying AI policy, economics, or infrastructure engineering, the MIIT plan, the EU AI Office competitiveness memo, and the US NIST AI Safety Institute reports all publish in English and none are behind paywalls. Start there before spending another hour on speculation.
